section.title: Retired Engineering Director: Netflix Culture, Hiring, Meta Leadership, and Work-Life Balance
section.deck: A retired engineering director who worked at Netflix and Facebook recounts how Netflix culture scaled, how he hired engineers, what he learned leading at Meta, and why a 2004 illness changed his view of work.

blocks.text: The host introduces David as a retired engineering director who worked at both Netflix and Facebook, and the conversation follows his 36-year career. In David's view, strong engineering organizations depend on three things: colleagues who are good to work with, a fair and objective way to record who did what, and a pace that leaves people a life outside work. He argues that engineering judgment matters more than LeetCode speed, that a new leader must earn trust before changing a team that already works, and that a serious illness in 2004 turned him against 24/7 work culture. Everything below is David's opinion or recollection from an auto-generated transcript, and several names and figures are unverified.
blocks.heading: David's view: judgment, trust, and balance matter more than heroics and long hours

blocks.question: How did Netflix differ from the other companies David had worked at?
answer: David says every earlier employer, from IBM through several smaller companies, tolerated prima donnas: very smart people who were hard to work with, who yelled at colleagues and customers, and who could not admit mistakes. He describes one 1990s engineer treated as indispensable, with a cubicle packed with junk, who avoided other people and fixed problems overnight while managers did not understand his work. When he quit, the company survived, and the rest of the team came to understand the area he had guarded.

At Netflix, David says, nobody was like that. The culture deck said the company did not hire brilliant jerks and would let go anyone difficult or unapproachable, however smart. David calls this revolutionary in the early 2000s and notes that the large tech companies he knows now work the same way.

His interview with Patty McCord, then chief people officer, who approved every hire at that small company, surprised him. David says she told him Netflix did not value 24/7 work and that he should impress the company with what he could do in an eight-hour day. David later watched a manager say he could not keep working around the clock. McCord thanked the manager, then told him not to do it again and to set up his team so that he did not have to. David calls that unthinkable in 2008 or 2009 and says he learned more about leading and collaborating from McCord than, he thinks, even from Reed Hastings.

David gives his own example. During early, unstable attempts at continuous deployment, a strong engineer remarked that David must enjoy having weekends off, because the systems would fail if the team stopped working. David told him in a one-on-one to take a vacation and said he did not care if things broke. The engineer took a week off, others rested too, and David says the team then stabilised the system quickly with its own approach.

David ends with Hastings. According to David, Hastings saw DVDs by mail as a stepping stone to streaming, which is why the company is not called DVDsbymail.com. Hastings was not a video expert but built a team of strong leaders and engineers to solve the problem.
blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: How did the Netflix culture change as the company grew?
answer: David first says the culture memo is aspirational. When people asked whether Netflix really worked that way, he answered that it described what the company aspired to be.

He then describes what failed to scale. Netflix credited the team, not individuals. When the company shipped on the PlayStation 3, David says, Sony's DVD division asked Netflix to stop because it had not designed the console for this, and Netflix carried on. Afterwards nobody named the foundational engineers; the credit went to Netflix. That worked when the company was small. As it took on many products, individual contributions got lost, and if engineers are not credited, he says, leaders collect the credit.

Netflix also had no engineering levels. Everyone was an engineer or a senior software engineer, and a business card could carry any title except manager, director, VP or chief. That suited an all-senior team. As it hired more juniors, David argues, teams contain strong, good and weak engineers, and without an objective way to tell them apart and reward wins, the best people leave. By the late 2010s he was arguing for levels. He assumes they have since been added, but he has been away for six years.

David adds that McCord interviewed almost every early hire and Hastings met a few new hires at a time, which could not continue as the company grew. When he left, he felt the memo suited a very small, aggressive, engineering-focused company.

followups.question: What is the culture memo?
answer: David describes a deck of roughly 15 slides, released around 2007 or 2008 by his recollection. Its ideas included no brilliant jerks, very smart people, inspiring people to sail the seas rather than telling them how to build a ship, top-of-market pay, and a "keeper test" under which the company fires aggressively. David calls it revolutionary at the time. In his reading it was about freedom and responsibility: hire excellent people, explain why the work matters, give context, and trust them to execute without micromanagement.
He adds that the talent was not limited to engineers. His HR partners challenged his hire and no-hire decisions, and he says he learned how to build a team from them.
followups.speaker: David

followups.question: If everyone was at the same level, how did Netflix pay people differently?
answer: David says Netflix generally did not hire new graduates, though he found ways around that. Pay followed a concept of personal top of market, and the memo encouraged people to interview elsewhere. His own starting salary in 2007 was $175,000, which he calls solid for then. If Google had offered him $200,000 a year later, he says, his manager would have had to match it or let him go. Leaders therefore had to track offers and market rates.

David says this became unsustainable. An engineer matched to a double-pay offer could, three years later, earn three times as much as a peer doing similar work, with no performance review or context to explain the gap. In another case, five candidates Netflix had made offers to each received Facebook offers about 1.2 times higher, the memo said to match, and without leveling nobody could justify it. He argued with his leadership using year-over-year spreadsheets and believes Netflix fixed this after he left, since a large company needs pay ranges.
followups.speaker: David

blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: How does David identify really strong software engineers in hiring?
answer: David says his hiring succeeded all the way up to Meta. Large companies such as Meta, Google, Amazon and Microsoft need structure and consistent standards, so they use a formal interview system. At smaller companies, when he made the hire or no-hire decision himself, he, three team members and HR interviewed each candidate.

He tells of a late-1990s candidate who had built driverless-train software. David was the last interviewer, and his 45-minute slot ran to 90 minutes, with two whiteboards covered in state transitions. He says her grasp of a complex system of interacting parts was among the best he had seen. Others gave her coding questions and she did fine, but the panel was lukewarm and his boss pushed back. David argued that the team was struggling to integrate disparate systems and needed her. They hired her, and he says she excelled. He claims his hiring record at small companies was close to perfect.

David knows his next view is controversial: he does not love LeetCode. He says it shows how fast someone can write code for a problem practiced many times. He accepts that at the volume Meta and Google hire, they have little alternative.

His alternative is an engineering foundation: understanding complex systems, strong technical intuition, and sound decisions without enough data. He has seen engineers from other fields do very well in software. He has also seen people who aced LeetCode and rehearsed system-design questions such as Google type-ahead get hired and then produce poor engineering, which he saw in their review packets. He believes this foundation is largely innate, like musical talent, and says he can help someone improve their software but cannot teach them to make good decisions.

His second story is about a project partner in graduate classes at San Jose State, taken in his 50s just before he joined Meta. She was finishing a master's in civil engineering, worked in wastewater treatment, and wanted to move into software. David was impressed by her analytical mind and command of statistics and wanted Netflix to hire her. Her take-home video-software task took three weeks and had rookie mistakes, so to help close the deal David suggested she teach the team something. She spent two hours at a whiteboard on wastewater treatment, and halfway through David realized he was watching a very complex state machine. A manager asked what sewage had to do with software but hired her, and later told David at a Meta event that she was doing very well. David says that when you see a brilliant engineering mind, LeetCode speed or building a scalable type-ahead does not matter, because those can be learned quickly.

David accepts that this approach does not scale at Meta or Google, where legal and policy problems would break it, so they set a bar and a level. His level advice is to take a lower offer: someone who was a 6 elsewhere and is offered a 5 at Meta should accept it and execute at the higher level, because bonuses, multipliers and refresh stock follow. An over-leveled hire who struggles has no clean fix. His rule is that when in doubt, go low and earn the quick promotion.

followups.question: How do you spot that fundamental engineering skill? Is there a question you ask?
answer: David says to interview the person, not the process. The wastewater candidate showed mastery of a hard engineering problem and explained it to engineers who knew nothing about it, until those who understood saw a finite state machine. He argues that many engineering systems, such as engines and other mechanical systems, reduce to states and transitions, though structural engineering differs.

Netflix would have hired her at a junior level, such as data analyst. As a full software engineer against the usual expectations she would have failed. A smaller company, he says, is flexible enough to hire and build up such a person.
followups.speaker: David

blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: Who was the strongest engineer David worked with, and what made that person strong?
answer: David names Giannis, though he usually avoids names. The captions garble the surname, so it is omitted here. They met in 2000 at InterVideo. Giannis had left the industry to teach signal processing in Greece, and in summer 2010 David brought him in during a break to help with ideas about parallel encoding. David says that work led to content-based encoding, which the whole industry now uses, and to an early patent.

Giannis later joined Netflix and, David says, took the idea further, in what the captions render as "convex all encoding", probably convex hull. David says it delivers the highest quality for a given bandwidth and is now the model at both Netflix and Meta. Giannis also built a cost-benefit model for codec evaluation. David sees his strength as forcing academic rigor into practice: decisions rest on tests across 10,000, a million or a billion videos, not on what two compressed videos suggest in theory.
blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: How did David come to be recruited to Meta?
answer: David says the early Netflix culture deck advised interviewing often to learn your market value. When Facebook contacted him in late 2017, as he recalls, he had not interviewed in about ten years. He went in, in his own words, a bit full of himself, citing how Netflix had built the highest-scale encoding platform. One interviewer told him Facebook could not solve its video scale problem with CPUs. David was floored, later thanked him, and realized he had understood video too narrowly. He got an offer and turned it down because he was not ready.

Soon after, Giannis told David about a Facebook offer and the custom chip (ASIC) work he would do. David saw a passion in him that he had not seen for a while. He thinks Netflix's culture, not built around individual contributions, may not have rewarded Giannis, and that the problems may not have seemed big enough to him. David says he did not try to talk Giannis out of it: as his boss he did not want to lose him, but as his friend he could not argue against it. David had been interviewing mainly to exercise his interview skills, but in the end he came to see Facebook's video work as a very hard problem. His team was solid and a successor was ready, so in 2019 he left Netflix, and Facebook offered him a job quickly.

At Netflix his encoding team had grown from one person to about 55, and trust grew with it. At Meta he took over a video processing team of 55 to 60 who did not know him. In an early meeting he talked about what needed work. A team member told him in a one-on-one that he had been there two weeks and was already telling the team what to do. David concluded he needed to stop talking and build trust, a skill he had never had to develop.

His lesson is that leadership is about relationships. If a team is broken, the leader's job is to fix it. If it is already executing well, the job is first not to break it and second to help it move forward, and he had jumped to the second step. David calls the saddest thing about Meta that it was his last job. He believes he would now be a much better organizational and engineering leader but no longer wants that responsibility, and he says he learned the most about engineering leadership there.

followups.question: Concretely, what does building trust look like for a senior leader joining an existing team?
answer: David says it meant slowing down and spending a lot of time in one-on-ones, asking questions, taking notes, and learning the system, the roles and the people. In a technical role, he says, a leader must understand why the team does what it does.

His first decision came when the team needed a manager. Many told him to promote an existing manager, but he did not know them and refused to decide just because it looked politically right. After taking time with them, he concluded an existing manager was the right choice. That manager had felt the role was his, so the relationship was difficult at first. David told him he was sorry for the delay but had needed to understand first, and that he was now confident in him. By the time the manager left Meta, David says, he no longer assumed the worst.
Looking back, David thinks his investment was still too small. He would tell his boss that for the first six months he was in school and that critical decisions would be made together.
followups.speaker: David

blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: What was David's favorite work or project at Meta?
answer: David first names bringing Netflix-level quality to Meta's scale, which he says succeeded. He then turns to COVID. He joined in late July 2019, and by March 2020 everyone was working from home. Meta planned for New Year's Eve from the summer because video traffic spiked for 24 hours. By April 2020, David says, every day looked like New Year's Eve in uploads, streams and live video. Systems that had never run at that sustained load were slowly bleeding out, with race conditions among the problems. He says the prime minister of India was addressing the country on Facebook Live, and he was terrified by the weight of it. The team worked from home, found the problems and resolved the race conditions. After about a month the systems and metrics held, and David says he was proud of that.

He also describes how his view of the company's value changed. He had first seen Facebook through a US-centric lens as a social app. He came to see what 3.5 billion customers means. By David's rough comparison, Netflix's roughly 300 million subscribers are the wealthiest 5 percent of the world by income, while Meta reaches the wealthiest 50 percent. He calls wealthy a loaded term, since at the bottom people live on about $68 a day. He says Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook are a lifeblood for small shops across India, and an Uber driver from Somalia in Seattle told him WhatsApp kept his scattered family in touch.

David says US debate about social media focuses on harms such as fake news and overlooks how much the products improve lives elsewhere. He believes the company changed lives by giving people a business, a platform to share and earn from video, and a way to stay close to family, and that it feels good to be part of that in a small way.
blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: How did work-life balance change across David's career?
answer: David says that in the late 1990s he worked hard for a visionary executive because the team was trying to catch up, not because anyone demanded it. At InterVideo, a startup, the expectation was 24/7. He arrived around 10:30 in the morning and left around 10 at night, sometimes at 2 or 3 in the morning, often seven days a week, chasing deals to lift the stock price after the IPO.

In January 2004 he fell ill on a Sunday and kept getting worse. On the Friday his wife took him to the emergency room, where, he says, a doctor said it was colon cancer, with a blockage that could kill quickly. He was in hospital for about three weeks with two surgeries and chemotherapy. It was stage three with lymph node spread, and he puts his five-year survival prognosis at about 25 percent. His children were two, four and seven, and he says the youngest barely knew him.

In hospital he decided that his way of working was wrong. He told his boss he still wanted the job but could not work that way, and he says that if a company threatens to fire you for not being there late, the best thing you can do is leave. He believes InterVideo used hours to cover for poor leadership. He calls work-life balance something thrust upon him, and he was determined never to be a leader who expects people to kill themselves for a job. Hearing at Netflix that the company did not value 24/7 work was a shock.

His advice is not to wait for cancer or a heart attack. Bake balance in early, take vacation, and leave the company alone for a week. If it cannot survive seven days without you, David says, that is its problem.

David says high-performance companies such as Meta and Netflix are often misunderstood. He recalls a Meta poster of a rocking horse that read, in effect, do not mistake motion for progress. He suggests agreeing with your boss on the most important work and telling the boss which tasks you will not do; if one matters, someone else must do it or priorities must change. Crunch time will come at big tech companies, but it should be the exception, planned in advance, such as a push in May and June followed by a vacation. He says balance is achievable even at Netflix or Meta, if the manager gives clear context.
blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: Which job taught David the most, and why?
answer: David says his last four jobs each contributed. The first turned him into a high-performance software engineer, performing by problems solved, not hours worked. The second gave him a video foundation. Netflix, he says, was zero to one, and there he learned leadership, hiring and firing, context setting and cross-functional work, which he brought to Meta.

What he lacked on arrival at Meta was an objective process for planning, reviews and performance. He calls the PSC performance cycle both his most dreaded and his favorite time of year. In his account, everyone writes a self-review, the manager builds a packet with feedback tied to goals, and managers then defend their engineers in calibration meetings. Each manager thinks their team is the best, David says, so the aim is to persuade with data about who deserves what level and who did what on a project. He valued getting each engineer's impact on paper. He says departing employees keep every performance package they were ever given.

David had heard horror stories about the performance cycle but found it mattered once inside. His greatest joy, he says, was giving a direct report a top rating, and he also valued helping people who were below expectations recover. He adds that he used to think he understood scale from books on sharding and microservices, but in his view those authors do not know scale at Meta's level. The most valuable thing he would bring to a new job is a system for objective planning, review and performance.
blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: Is there a top book that influenced David's career?
answer: David chooses a late-1990s book he names as 12 Secrets to Microsoft Success; the title comes from auto-generated captions and was not checked. He says it described radical thinking at Microsoft. One idea was betting the company, which he says he saw at Netflix, Amazon and Meta when a big opportunity is worth risking the company on without going all-in. Another was good failure: in a healthy company, projects and people will fail, and what counts is how you fail, what you learn and whether the bet was reasonable and managed early.

As he recalls the book, Microsoft was the first company to say publicly that it aimed to hire the top 5 percent of software engineers, and it coined the term dogfooding. When the NT server was failing badly in the mid-1990s, he says, Bill Gates made the whole company move to it, which put the bugs in front of everyone and got them fixed. After rapid growth Gates also imposed a company-wide hiring freeze because people were working on things that did not matter, such as Microsoft Bob. Executives were forced to kill projects, and David says the bottom 20 percent were cut, which he thinks should have happened anyway.

David says Microsoft set early models for modern engineering leadership, and others borrowed from it. Before the 2022 crash he thought the hiring rate did not add up. During COVID everyone accelerated hiring and nobody slowed. He believes that had big-tech leaders read the book, they would have seen in late 2021 that hiring was out of control.
blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: Is there anything David regrets that others could learn from?
answer: David says his first six years out of school were wasted at very large failing companies. He names Hughes, spun off from General Motors, and an IBM division sold to Siemens, both of which failed. He had a good salary and an easy job, thought only about the moment, and did not think about growth. He does not mean being ambitious about a vice-president title in ten years, just thinking about growth.

For software engineers in particular, he says, everything learned will be obsolete in about five years. When he joined Meta, the bootcamp and the whole development environment had been replaced; he had been proficient as a director, but when he later went to an individual-contributor role he found everything had changed. His way of staying successful, David says, is to keep pushing toward the edge and keep learning new engineering skills.
blocks.speaker: David

blocks.question: What advice would David give himself at the start of his career?
answer: First, work on hard problems. David says that if the job is not difficult, you are not growing. Once a role flatlines, he says, an engineer at a company like Meta, where moving internally is easy, should find another hard problem. Hard problems are what move engineers forward.

Second, company size does not matter, but everyone should work at a small company or startup at some point, ideally while young. He cautions against being too taken with the technology and says to work for visionary leaders who can also execute, since vision without execution goes nowhere. He cites Zuckerberg and Hastings as visionary, and says Hastings was one in 1999, when Netflix had four people. Leaders should make you dream of sailing the seas, not just cut lumber for a ship.
Third, plan for work-life balance deliberately from the first job. Work and life are in tension, he says, but the best engineering comes from people who love the work and also enjoy time off.

Fourth, start financial planning on day one, because as technical people succeed they earn more and, without a plan, will not know where it goes. David recommends a deliberate plan for spending and for short- and long-term savings, small regular contributions in your 20s, and no extended credit or debt. He says that by the early 40s this will not usually allow retirement unless you were lucky, as with an early job at Facebook or Netflix, but it can give financial independence, so you could take a lower-paying job. In his view a 401(k) alone and Social Security will not be enough for those who start late. He knows many engineers in their 50s who earned well but have no plan, and says a good engineer employed for 30 to 35 years has no reason not to retire comfortably. He says elsewhere that he is not a financial planner, so this is one person's opinion.
blocks.speaker: David
